title: Adding Up an Arithmetic Sequence
idea: Write an arithmetic series forwards and backwards and every column adds to first plus last, so Sₙ = n/2 (u₁ + uₙ); putting in uₙ = u₁ + (n − 1)d gives the second form, Sₙ = n/2 (2u₁ + (n − 1)d).
misconceptions: Using n instead of n − 1 inside the formula: n/2(2u_1 + nd)
Using the wrong n, such as the last term's value or the number of gaps
Finding u_n when the question asks for S_n (or the reverse)

estimate.basis: 150 spoken words a minute, plus each pause, 0.8 s for each cue and 2 s for each tap question with its longer feedback line. The two figures are the two recall versions. Player turns are player-paced and not counted.

notes: leads_to and builds_on match the explainer map (FAL-952). The map's entry is SL1.2.sum only, as this pilot teaches it; example 2 finds n from the last term on the way. Finding an unknown from a given sum is ex.algebra.arithmetic-sum-unknown.

The two forms of the formula are the two methods (task FAL-936). Gauss pairing is the big idea, not a third method, and the GDC routes (sum(seq(…)), cumulative lists) belong in a method explainer under plan decision 4.

Example 1 uses the fight pit from ex.algebra.arithmetic-sequence, and its check uses row 40 = 178 seats from there, so a player who watched both sees the two lessons join up. A player who didn't still gets every number on the board.

Format 2 (FAL-1043): moved from approved back to draft until it passes the format 2 checks (#188, #190, #191). `node tools/explainer-scripts.mjs --todo` lists what is left: turn lines with numbers or story words, not-yet lines to key to misconceptions, repeated frames and jokes, and the figure.
Waits for the figure board item (README, "Figures"): Gauss's two lined-up rows are text drawings.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Mags again. The pit boss is selling every seat for the big fight, and he wants the house counted before the gates open.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Last time he counted seats himself, he got as far as row nine and needed a lie-down.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Forty rows, every seat, and we won't count one.

ask.prompt: An arithmetic sequence has u₁ = 7 and d = 5. Find u₂₀.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: One hundred and two. Nineteen hops of five on top of seven. Keep that formula close. We're building on it.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Nineteen hops from the first term to the twentieth. Nineteen fives are ninety-five, and seven more is one hundred and two.

not_watched.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_watched.say: Quick one before we start. Tap the answer.

ask.prompt: An arithmetic sequence has u₁ = 7 and d = 5. Find u₂₀.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: It's one hundred and two. Here's why.

not_watched.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_watched.say: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount, d, every time. To get term n, start at the first term and add d, n minus one times. n minus one, because you count the hops between the terms, not the terms. So u n is u one, plus n minus one lots of d.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: There's an old story from before the dust. A boy called Carl Gauss was told to add up every number from one to a hundred, to keep him quiet.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: The way the story goes, he wrote the sum out forwards, and underneath it, backwards. Then he added each column.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: One and a hundred, a hundred and one. Two and ninety-nine, a hundred and one. Every column comes to a hundred and one.

ask.prompt: Why does every column add to the same total?
choices: Along the top each number goes up by 1, and along the bottom each goes down by 1

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: That's it. What the top row gains, the bottom row loses, so the column total holds steady.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Watch one column to the next. The top number goes up one and the bottom one comes down one. They cancel.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: A hundred columns of a hundred and one is ten thousand, one hundred. But every number's in there twice, so halve it. Five thousand and fifty.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: It didn't keep him quiet for long.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Two words for the book. Add up the terms of a sequence and you get a series. S n is the sum of the first n terms.

board.write: series: the terms of a sequence added up
Sₙ = u₁ + u₂ + … + uₙ, the sum of the first n terms

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: The trick works on any arithmetic series. Every column is first plus last, and there are n columns. Then halve it, because everything's written twice.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: That's one form. Swap u n for what it equals, u one plus n minus one lots of d, and you get the other. n over two, times two u one plus n minus one lots of d.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Both are in the formula book. Same sum, two doors in. Pick your door by what you've got.

problem.setup: Row 1 of the fight pit has 22 seats, and each row has 4 more seats than the row in front of it. Find the total number of seats in the first 40 rows.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Back to the pit. Step one: what are we finding? The total of the first forty rows. That's S forty, not u forty.

board.write: Find S₄₀, the total number of seats in rows 1 to 40.
board.label: Step 1: what are we finding?

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step two: the givens, with units. u one, twenty-two seats. d, four seats per row. n, forty rows.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step three: pick the door. We know d, but we haven't worked out the back row, so it's the d form. Formula first.

board.write: We know d, not u₄₀: use the d form.
board.label: Step 3: pick the formula

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step four: substitute. Forty over two, times two twenty-twos plus forty minus one lots of four.

ask.prompt: Why is there a 40/2 at the front?
choices: Forwards and backwards writes every seat twice, so we halve

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: That's it. The trick writes the sum down twice, so we halve it.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Think back to forwards and backwards. Every seat got written down twice. Halving gives the real total.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step five: work it out. Two twenty-twos, forty-four. Thirty-nine fours, a hundred and fifty-six. Together that's two hundred. Twenty lots of two hundred: four thousand.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step six, in words: the first forty rows hold four thousand seats.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Check it's sensible. Four thousand over forty rows is a hundred a row, on average. That's halfway between twenty-two at the front and a hundred and seventy-eight at the back.

board.write: Check: 4000 ÷ 40 = 100 a row, halfway between 22 and u₄₀ = 178 ✓

parts.text: Find the total number of seats in the first 25 rows.

working: u₁ = 30 seats, d = 3 seats per row, n = 25

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Right formula, right total. Into the book.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: You picked the formula before you touched a number. Good habit.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Inside the bracket it's n minus one lots of d. Count the hops.

problem.setup: A failing well gives 480 litres on day 1, and 15 litres less on each day after that. The crew stops drawing water after the day it gives 195 litres. Find the total amount of water the crew draws.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: A harder one. The old well: four hundred and eighty litres on day one, fifteen less each day. The crew stops after the day it gives a hundred and ninety-five. What did they draw, all told?

board.write: Find Sₙ, the total water drawn.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: We know the last term. We don't know n, the number of days. So first: which term is a hundred and ninety-five? Set the formula for u n equal to it.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Take four eighty from both sides: minus two hundred and eighty-five. Divide both sides by minus fifteen. n minus one is nineteen.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: We've got the first term and the last, so it's first plus last. Which number goes in for n?

ask.prompt: n − 1 = 19. In Sₙ = n/2 (u₁ + uₙ), n = ?

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Twenty. n counts the days. Nineteen hops, twenty days.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Nineteen is the hops, and a hundred and ninety-five is the litres. n counts the days: twenty.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: So n is twenty.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Twenty over two is ten. Four eighty and one ninety-five is six hundred and seventy-five. Ten of those: six thousand, seven hundred and fifty litres.

problem.setup: A barricade is built from sandbags in layers. Layer 1, at the bottom, has 96 sandbags, and each layer above it has 4 fewer sandbags than the layer below. The barricade has 18 layers.

parts.text: Find the number of sandbags in the top layer.
Find the total number of sandbags in the barricade.
Show that the total number of sandbags in the first n layers is 98n − 2n².

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Old exam layout now: letters down, each part's working under it. A barricade of eighteen layers, ninety-six sandbags at the bottom and four fewer in each layer up.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Part a. The top layer is layer eighteen. Ninety-six, plus seventeen lots of minus four. Seventeen fours are sixty-eight, so that's twenty-eight.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Part b. We've found the last term, so first plus last is the quick door. Use your answer from part a, even if you're not sure of it. Whoever marks it follows your working through.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Eighteen over two is nine. Ninety-six and twenty-eight make a hundred and twenty-four. Nine of those is one thousand, one hundred and sixteen sandbags.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Part c says show that. They've given you the answer. Your job is to get there from the formula, step by step, and land exactly on their line. Keep n as n, and never work backwards.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: We want it in terms of n, so the d form. Two ninety-sixes are a hundred and ninety-two. The bracket gives minus four n plus four. That's a hundred and ninety-six minus four n.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Multiply through by n over two. Ninety-eight n, minus two n squared. That's their line, so we stop.

ask.prompt: Why not put n = 18 into 98n − 2n², get 1116, and stop?
choices: One value doesn't show it's true for every n

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Right. One number's a check, not a proof. Do the check on scrap, and show it in general on the page.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Eighteen only tells you it works for eighteen. Show that wants every n, so you work in general. Eighteen makes a good check on scrap.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: On scrap, then. Eighteen gives one thousand, one hundred and sixteen, same as part b. The parts agree.

sections.about: Part (b) of example 3 again, the two forms side by side.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Back to part b, through the other door. Same question, the form with d in it. Side by side.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Look inside the brackets. One ninety-two take sixty-eight is a hundred and twenty-four, same as first plus last. Two u one plus n minus one lots of d is first plus last, written another way.

ask.prompt: When is Method 1, n/2 (u₁ + uₙ), the one to pick?
choices: When you know the last term
When you know d but not the last term

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: That's it. Last term in hand, use it.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Method one needs u n. Got the last term? Use it.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Only d and n? The d form. Want it in terms of n, like part c? The d form again.

board.write: Know d, not uₙ, or need it in terms of n → METHOD 2: n/2 (2u₁ + (n − 1)d)

sections.misconception: Using n instead of n − 1 inside the formula: n/2(2u_1 + nd)

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Somebody's tallied the pit and got it wrong. One line's off. Find it.

ask.prompt: Tap the line with the slip.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: That one. Forty lots of four, where it should be thirty-nine.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Look inside the bracket on the first line. How many lots of d should there be?

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Two checks would have caught it. Put n equals one in, and the sum of one term has to be the first term. Their rule gives twenty-four, not twenty-two.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Or work it the other way. First plus last gives four thousand. Two methods, two different answers? Somebody's lying.

intro.speaker: mags-the-ledger
intro.say: Your turn. No help on the first go. Label every part, and pick your formula before you write a number.

fallback.setup: A salvage crew hauls 40 kg of scrap on day 1, and 6 kg more on each day after that.

parts.text: Find the amount of scrap the crew hauls on day 15.
Find the total amount of scrap hauled over the first 15 days.
Show that the total hauled over the first n days is 3n² + 37n kg.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Every part labelled, and the parts agree. I'd sign that.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Clean books. Nothing for me to cross out.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Are you after one day, or all of them added up? Check which the part asks for.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: For the show that, start from the formula with d in it and keep n as n.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: So. A series is a sequence added up. Forwards and backwards, every column is first plus last, so it's n over two, first plus last. No last term? Use the d form.

board.write: Sₙ = n/2 (u₁ + uₙ): you know the last term
Check: S₁ = u₁, and both doors agree
